title: n8n: Workflow Automation That Puts You in Control
description: Learn n8n, the open-source workflow automation platform, from your first workflow to AI-powered agents. Self-hosting, core building blocks, LLM integration, RAG, and production-grade debugging and error handling.

lessons.title: What Workflow Automation Actually Is
lessons.bodyMd:
## The boring work tax

Every builder pays it. Copying a new lead's email from a form into a spreadsheet. Checking a dashboard every morning for the same number. Sending the same "thanks for signing up" message fifty times a week. None of this work is hard. All of it eats your day.

Workflow automation is the practice of handing that repetitive work to software. Instead of you moving data between apps by hand, you define the route once, and the machine runs it every time.

## What counts as a workflow

A workflow is just a sequence: when THIS happens, do THAT, then THAT.

- When a customer pays (the trigger), add them to your email list, send a welcome message, and log the sale in a spreadsheet (the actions).
- When a contact form is submitted, score the lead, notify your team in Slack, and create a follow-up task.
- Every morning at 7 AM, pull yesterday's numbers and email yourself a summary.

Each workflow has three parts: a trigger (what starts it), steps (what happens in order), and data (what flows between the steps). That is the whole game. Everything else in this guide is detail.

## Why beginners win fast here

You do not need to be a programmer to start. n8n is visual: you drag boxes onto a canvas and connect them with lines. But unlike simpler tools, n8n also lets you drop into real JavaScript when you need it, which means your skills grow with the tool instead of outgrowing it.

## The compounding effect

A task that takes you ten minutes a day costs you about sixty hours a year. Automate five of those and you have bought back more than a month of working time. That is why automation is one of the highest-leverage skills a builder can learn: the work you do once keeps paying you forever.

## What you will build in this guide

By the end, you will have built real workflows: a morning briefing that pulls live data from an API, a lead pipeline that routes and notifies your team, an AI agent that answers questions using your own documents, and the error handling that keeps it all running while you sleep.

## A note on how to use this guide

Each lesson ends with something you can try in your own n8n instance within minutes. Do the trying. Automation is a hands-on skill: reading about a webhook is worth a tenth of firing one and watching your workflow catch it. Keep a scratch workflow called "Playground" where you test every new node before trusting it in something real.

Let us start with what n8n is and why it exists.

lessons.title: n8n vs Zapier vs Make
lessons.bodyMd:
## The big three

If you have looked at automation tools, you have seen three names: Zapier, Make, and n8n. They all connect apps and move data. They differ in price, power, and philosophy. Here is the honest breakdown.

## Zapier: the easy button

Zapier is the most beginner-friendly and has the largest app library (7,000+ integrations). If you want "when someone fills out my Typeform, add them to Mailchimp" done in five minutes, Zapier is lovely.

The tradeoffs: it gets expensive fast, because you pay per task (every single step counts). Complex branching logic is painful. Your data flows through Zapier's servers, always. And you cannot self-host it or look at the source code. It is a black box you rent.

## Make: the visual powerhouse

Make (formerly Integromat) gives you a beautiful visual canvas with powerful branching, looping, and data tools. Its free tier is generous, and pricing per operation is fairer than Zapier for multi-step scenarios.

The tradeoffs: it is still closed source and cloud-only. At high volumes the operation-based pricing still adds up. And while it has added AI features, AI agents are not its native strength.

## n8n: the builder's choice

n8n is open source and can be self-hosted, which means your data never has to leave your own server. Pricing is based on workflow executions, not individual steps, so a 20-step workflow costs the same as a 2-step one. It has 400+ built-in integrations plus a generic HTTP Request node that can talk to any API on earth. It has first-class AI agent nodes. And when the visual editor is not enough, you can write real JavaScript in a Code node.

The tradeoff: the learning curve is steeper. Self-hosting means you own updates, backups, and uptime. There is more to learn, which is exactly what this guide is for.

## Side-by-side

| | Zapier | Make | n8n |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ease of use | Easiest | Medium | Medium-steep |
| Self-hosting | No | No | Yes |
| Open source | No | No | Yes |
| Pricing model | Per task (step) | Per operation | Per execution |
| AI agents | Basic | Growing | Native, deep |
| Custom code | Limited | Limited | Full JavaScript/Python |
| Data privacy | Vendor servers | Vendor servers | Your server if self-hosted |

## The bottom line

Pick Zapier when you need one simple automation done in the next ten minutes and never want to think about infrastructure. Pick Make when you want visual power on a budget. Pick n8n when you want control: your data, your server, your code, AI agents, and pricing that does not punish you for building sophisticated workflows.

If you are reading this guide, you have already decided you want the control. Good choice. Let us make it pay off.

lessons.title: When n8n Is the Right Choice
lessons.bodyMd:
## n8n shines when...

Not every job needs n8n. Here is where it genuinely earns its place.

**You care where your data lives.** If you automate anything with customer data, financial records, or health-adjacent information, self-hosting n8n means that data never passes through a third-party automation vendor. For many businesses, that alone settles the decision.

**Your workflows are getting expensive elsewhere.** A lead pipeline with enrichment, scoring, CRM writes, and notifications can easily be 8 to 12 steps. On per-step pricing, hundreds of leads a day becomes hundreds of dollars a month. On n8n, one execution is one execution no matter how many steps it has.

**You want AI agents, not just AI text boxes.** n8n's AI Agent node can use tools, call your other workflows, query your database, and ask a human for approval before acting. That is a different league from "summarize this text" buttons.

**You hit the walls of no-code.** The moment you think "I wish I could just write a little script here," n8n lets you. The Code node runs JavaScript (and Python on self-hosted setups), so there is always an escape hatch.

**You want to own your stack.** Open source means no vendor lock-in on the platform itself. Your workflows export as JSON. You can move them, version them in git, and run them anywhere.

## n8n is overkill when...

Honesty matters. Skip n8n (for now) if you need exactly one simple automation, like syncing new Shopify orders to a spreadsheet, and you will never touch it again. Zapier will do that in five minutes with less learning.

Also skip self-hosting if you have zero interest in running a server. n8n Cloud exists precisely for this: you get the power of n8n without the ops work, at a fair price.

## The sweet spot for this guide's audience

You are a beginner-to-intermediate builder. You want to automate real business processes, add AI where it helps, and understand what is happening under the hood. You would rather learn one powerful tool deeply than juggle five shallow ones.

That is the n8n sweet spot. In the next lesson, we will build the mental model you need before touching the canvas.

## A quick self-test

Answer these three questions honestly:

1. Do you have at least one repetitive task that involves two or more apps? (Email to spreadsheet, form to CRM, anything you copy-paste weekly.) If yes, you have your first workflow candidate.
2. Are you comfortable learning a tool over a weekend rather than demanding five-minute setup? n8n rewards a little patience with a lot of power.
3. Do you want AI in your automations, not just beside them? If the answer is yes, n8n's agent nodes are the most practical on-ramp available.

Three yeses: you are in the right place. Mixed answers: still fine, start with n8n Cloud and the simple workflows in Chapter 2, and let the harder chapters wait until you feel the pull.

lessons.title: How n8n Thinks: The Mental Model
lessons.bodyMd:
## Workflows, nodes, and executions

n8n has a small vocabulary. Learn these five words and the whole tool clicks.

**Workflow.** A workflow is one automation: a set of connected steps that runs from start to finish. "Morning briefing," "lead router," and "support ticket triage" are each one workflow.

**Node.** A node is one box on the canvas that does one job. There are trigger nodes (they start workflows), action nodes (they do things, like sending an email or calling an API), logic nodes (they branch, merge, and loop), and AI nodes (they think). You will meet all of them in Chapter 3.

**Trigger.** Every workflow starts with exactly one trigger. A trigger is the event that kicks things off: a schedule ("every day at 7 AM"), a webhook (someone POSTs data to a URL), or an app event ("new email arrived").

**Item.** Data flows between nodes as items. An item is just a JSON object, like `{"name": "Maya", "email": "maya@example.com"}`. Most nodes process every item they receive, one by one, automatically. If a node gets ten items, it runs its job ten times. You rarely need a loop for this, which surprises beginners.

**Execution.** One run of a workflow is an execution. When your 7 AM schedule fires, that is one execution. When a webhook receives a POST, that is one execution. n8n's pricing and monitoring both revolve around executions, so the word matters.

## The canvas is a pipeline

Picture water flowing through pipes. The trigger is the faucet. Each node is a station that transforms the water: filters it, splits it into two streams, heats it, bottles it. The lines between nodes are the pipes, carrying items from one station to the next.

When you look at the n8n canvas, read it left to right: trigger on the left, data flowing rightward through each node. Click any node after a test run and you will see exactly what data went in and what came out. That input/output inspector is your best friend while learning.

## Active vs. inactive

A workflow you are building is inactive: it only runs when you press the manual "execute" button for testing. When you flip it to active, the trigger goes live: schedules start firing, webhooks start listening. This two-state design is a safety feature. You test while inactive, then activate when you trust it.

## Pinned data: your rehearsal tool

Here is a beginner superpower: after a test run, you can "pin" a node's output data. From then on, downstream nodes reuse that pinned data instead of re-running the upstream steps. This lets you test node 8 of your workflow a hundred times without re-firing the webhook or re-calling the API at node 1. We will use this constantly in Chapter 5's debugging lesson.

## The one-sentence summary

A trigger starts an execution, items flow through nodes left to right, each node transforms the data, and you test while inactive before going live. Hold that picture. In Chapter 2, you will get n8n running and build your first real workflow.

lessons.title: Starting with n8n Cloud
lessons.bodyMd:
## The fastest path: n8n Cloud

If you want to learn n8n without managing a server, start with n8n Cloud at n8n.io. You get a free trial, and your instance is running in about a minute. No Docker, no terminal, no infrastructure decisions. For this entire guide, Cloud and self-hosted behave the same in the editor, so everything you learn transfers.

## Signing up

1. Go to n8n.io and start the trial.
2. Pick a workspace name. This becomes part of your instance URL, like `yourname.app.n8n.cloud`.
3. Verify your email and sign in. You land on the workflows dashboard.

That is genuinely it. Your n8n is live.

## What the trial gives you

The trial includes a generous batch of workflow executions so you can build and test freely. Paid Cloud plans scale from starter (a few thousand executions a month) upward. Remember the pricing superpower from Chapter 1: you pay per execution, not per step. A 15-node workflow that runs 100 times costs the same as a 2-node workflow that runs 100 times. Design accordingly: do not be afraid of adding steps that make your workflow smarter.

## Your first look around

Click "Create Workflow" (or open the starter template). You will see the canvas: an empty space with a "+" button. Clicking it reveals the trigger panel. We will build your first workflow in Lesson 3 of this chapter, but take a minute now to click around. Nothing here can break anything while the workflow is inactive.

## When to consider self-hosting later

Cloud is the right default while learning. Consider moving to self-hosted when any of these become true: your execution volume makes Cloud pricing uncomfortable, you have data-residency or compliance requirements, or you simply want full control. The next lesson walks through self-hosting with Docker, and migrating is easy: export any workflow as JSON from Cloud and import it into your self-hosted instance.

## One decision to make now

Cloud or self-hosted is the only real fork in the road, and you can switch later. If you chose Cloud, skip the next lesson and meet me at Lesson 3, where we build your first workflow. If you chose self-hosted, the next lesson gets your server running.

## What to do in your first 15 minutes

Do not try to build something ambitious yet. Instead, get comfortable with the feel of the tool:

1. Create a blank workflow and add a Manual Trigger (the "play button" trigger for testing).
2. Add a Set node after it and give it two fields: your name and today's date as static text.
3. Press "Execute workflow" and watch both nodes light up green.
4. Click the Set node and inspect the output. That input/output inspector is where you will spend half your n8n life.

Nothing you do here can break anything. The workflow is inactive, no credentials are involved, and no data leaves your instance. Play freely: drag nodes around, delete them with Ctrl+Z to undo, rename a node by double-clicking its title. Comfort with the canvas now saves frustration later.

lessons.title: Self-Hosting n8n with Docker
lessons.bodyMd:
## Why self-host

Self-hosting means n8n runs on your own machine or server. Your workflow data never touches n8n's servers. There is no per-execution bill from n8n itself (you just pay for whatever server you run it on, which can be a $5/month VPS or even your laptop for learning). And you get extras Cloud does not allow, like importing any npm package in the Code node.

The price: you own updates, backups, and keeping it online. For learning, running it on your own computer with Docker is perfect.

## Prerequisites

You need Docker installed. On Mac or Windows, install Docker Desktop. On Linux, install Docker Engine. Verify it works:

```bash
docker --version
```

If that prints a version number, you are ready.

## Running n8n in one command

```bash
docker run -d \
  --name n8n \
  -p 5678:5678 \
  -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n \
  n8nio/n8n
```

What this does: `-d` runs it in the background, `--name n8n` names the container, `-p 5678:5678` maps the port so you can open it in your browser, `-v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n` creates a persistent volume so your workflows survive restarts, and `n8nio/n8n` is the official image.

Open http://localhost:5678 in your browser. Create your owner account on first launch. You now have n8n.

## A cleaner setup with Docker Compose

For anything beyond experimenting, use a compose file. Save this as `docker-compose.yml`:

```yaml
services:
  n8n:
    image: n8nio/n8n
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "5678:5678"
    environment:
      - N8N_BASIC_AUTH_ACTIVE=true
      - N8N_BASIC_AUTH_USER=admin
      - N8N_BASIC_AUTH_PASSWORD=change-this-password
      - GENERIC_TIMEZONE=America/Chicago
      - TZ=America/Chicago
    volumes:
      - n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n

volumes:
  n8n_data:
```

Then run `docker compose up -d`. The environment variables add basic-auth login protection and set your timezone so schedule triggers fire when you expect.

## Keeping it healthy

**Updates:** every week or two, run `docker compose pull && docker compose up -d`. n8n ships fixes constantly.

**Backups:** your workflows live in the `n8n_data` volume. Back it up with `docker run --rm -v n8n_data:/data -v $(pwd):/backup busybox tar czf /backup/n8n-backup.tar.gz /data`. Also export critical workflows as JSON from the UI (workflow menu, Download) and keep them in git.

**Going public:** if you want webhooks reachable from the internet, put n8n behind HTTPS. The simplest path is a reverse proxy like Caddy, which handles certificates automatically. Never expose an unauthenticated n8n instance to the internet.

## Troubleshooting first launch

Port already in use? Change `"5678:5678"` to `"5679:5678"` and open port 5679. Container exits immediately? Check logs with `docker logs n8n`. Forgot your login? The owner account is created on first launch, so worst case, stop the container, delete the volume, and start fresh while you are still learning.

You now have a running n8n. Next lesson: your first real workflow.

lessons.title: Your First Workflow: A Morning Briefing
lessons.bodyMd:
## What we are building

A morning briefing workflow: every day at 7 AM, it fetches the current weather from a free API that needs no signup, formats a friendly message, and shows you the result. You will touch a trigger, an HTTP node, and a Code node: the three most common node types in n8n.

## Step 1: Add a Schedule trigger

1. Create a new workflow.
2. Click the "+" on the canvas and choose "Schedule Trigger" (under "On a schedule").
3. Set it to run every day at 7:00. Leave the timezone on your local setting.

This trigger fires the workflow on schedule. One schedule fire equals one execution.

## Step 2: Fetch live weather data

1. Click "+", search for "HTTP Request", and add it.
2. Set Method to GET.
3. Set the URL to the free Open-Meteo API (no key needed). This example uses Chicago; swap in your own coordinates:

```
https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=41.88&longitude=-87.63&current=temperature_2m,weather_code&temperature_unit=fahrenheit&timezone=auto
```

4. Click "Execute step". You will see JSON come back with a `current` object containing the temperature. Congratulations: your workflow just talked to the real internet.

## Step 3: Format it with a Code node

1. Add a "Code" node after the HTTP Request.
2. Paste this JavaScript:

```js
const current = $input.first().json.current;
const temp = Math.round(current.temperature_2m);

const messages = [
  `Good morning. It is ${temp}F outside right now.`,
  `Rise and shine. Current temp: ${temp}F.`,
  `Morning briefing: ${temp}F and counting.`
];
const pick = messages[Math.floor(Math.random() * messages.length)];

return [{ json: { briefing: pick, tempF: temp } }];
```

3. Execute the step. The output panel shows your formatted briefing text.

You just used an expression-free Code node: `$input.first().json` grabs the incoming data, plain JavaScript transforms it, and returning an array of `{json: ...}` objects passes items downstream.

## Step 4: See the whole thing run

Click "Execute workflow" at the bottom. Watch each node light up as items flow through. Click any node to inspect what went in and what came out. That is a complete n8n workflow: trigger, fetch, transform.

## Making it actually useful

Right now the briefing just sits in the output panel. To get it delivered, add a fourth node: Gmail ("Send message"), Slack ("Send message"), or even the "Send Email" SMTP node. You will need to connect a credential, which we cover in Chapter 5. For now, notice the pattern you have learned: trigger, get data, shape data, deliver data. Nearly every workflow you will ever build follows this shape.

## Save and (optionally) activate

Save the workflow with a clear name like "Morning Weather Briefing". Leave it inactive while you experiment. When you add a delivery node and trust it, flip it to Active and it will run every morning on its own.

Three nodes, one real automation. In the next lesson, we tour the interface so you know where everything lives.

lessons.title: A Tour of the n8n Interface
lessons.bodyMd:
## The canvas

The big empty space is the canvas. This is where workflows live. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom. Nodes are the boxes, connections are the lines between them. Data flows left to right. The "+" button between nodes lets you insert a node into an existing connection without rewiring.

At the bottom of the canvas: "Execute workflow" runs the whole thing manually for testing. Each node also has its own "Execute step" for testing one node at a time. Use per-node execution constantly while building.

## The node panel

Clicking "+" opens the node panel with a search bar. Nodes are grouped: triggers ("On a schedule", "Webhook", app triggers), actions (every app integration), logic ("If", "Switch", "Merge", "Code", "Set"), and AI nodes. There is also a "Templates" tab with thousands of community workflows you can import and study. When you are stuck, searching templates for your use case is one of the fastest ways to learn.

## The input/output inspector

Click any node after a test run to see two panels: INPUT (what arrived) and OUTPUT (what it produced). You can switch between Table, JSON, and Schema views. Table view is friendliest for beginners. This inspector is how you debug everything: if a node misbehaves, the answer is always visible here.

## The left sidebar

The sidebar holds: Workflows (your list), Credentials (API keys and logins, stored securely), Variables (reusable values), and Executions (the history of every run). We will use Executions heavily in Chapter 5.

## Workflow settings

Click the three dots next to the workflow name for settings. The important ones for now:

- **Save:** n8n autosaves, but get in the habit of checking.
- **Download/Import:** export the workflow as JSON. Do this before big changes.
- **Settings:** timezone, timeout, and the error workflow assignment (Chapter 5).
- **Notes:** Shift+N or right-click to add a sticky note. Future you will thank present you for documenting tricky logic.

## Keyboard shortcuts worth learning

- `Ctrl/Cmd + S`: save
- `Ctrl/Cmd + Z`: undo (yes, it works on the canvas)
- `Delete`: remove selected nodes
- `Ctrl/Cmd + click`: select multiple nodes to move or copy them together
- `Tab` then type: quick-add a node

## Credentials: a first look

Open Credentials in the sidebar and click "Create". You will see every app n8n supports: Gmail, Slack, OpenAI, Postgres, and hundreds more. Each credential stores the login once, securely, and any workflow can reference it without ever seeing the raw secret. You will create your first real credential in Chapter 3 when we send data somewhere.

You now know your way around. Time for the building blocks: triggers, nodes, data flow, and expressions.

lessons.title: Triggers: How Workflows Start
lessons.bodyMd:
## Triggers answer one question: "when?"

Every workflow begins with a trigger. The trigger decides when an execution starts and what data it starts with. Choose the trigger first, because everything downstream depends on it.

## The four trigger families

**1. Schedule.** "Run every X." Every hour, every day at 7 AM, every Monday. Perfect for reports, syncs, reminders, and cleanup jobs. The workflow starts with empty input data; it goes out and fetches what it needs.

**2. Webhook.** "Run when someone calls this URL." n8n gives you a unique URL. Any system that can send an HTTP request (a form, your website, another app, another n8n workflow) can trigger it and include data in the payload. This is how n8n receives the outside world in real time.

**3. App triggers.** "Run when something happens in this app." New email in Gmail, new row in Google Sheets, new Stripe payment. Under the hood these are either webhooks (instant, the app pushes to n8n) or polling (n8n checks every few minutes). Instant beats polling when both exist.

**4. Manual and special triggers.** "Execute workflow" for testing, "Execute Sub-workflow" when another workflow calls this one, "Error Trigger" for error-handling workflows (Chapter 5), and the Chat trigger for conversational AI workflows (Chapter 4).

## Webhooks in practice

Add a Webhook node as your trigger. n8n shows two URLs: a test URL and a production URL. While building, use the test URL: click "Listen for test event," then send data to it (with curl, Postman, or your form). The workflow captures that payload, and you build against real data. When you activate the workflow, switch to the production URL.

A typical webhook payload looks like this:

```json
{
  "name": "Jordan",
  "email": "jordan@example.com",
  "company": "Acme Inc",
  "message": "Interested in a demo"
}
```

Every downstream node can now use `{{ $json.email }}` to reach that email. Webhooks are the front door of serious automation: lead forms, payment notifications, and app-to-app handoffs all arrive this way.

## Securing your webhooks

A webhook URL is a public door. Anyone with the URL can knock. For anything beyond experiments:

- In the Webhook node settings, set authentication (header auth or basic auth) and require callers to send a secret.
- Or verify a signature in the first Code node and stop the workflow if it does not match.

Never leave a production webhook that writes to your CRM or sends emails wide open.

## Polling vs. instant: a practical rule

If the app offers an instant trigger (it says "trigger" rather than polling in n8n's node list), use it: faster and fewer wasted executions. Polling triggers run on a schedule and check for new items; they consume executions even when nothing changed. For a "new email" workflow, instant Gmail push beats polling every 5 minutes.

## Choosing your trigger: a cheat sheet

- Daily/weekly job (reports, digests, cleanup): Schedule.
- Real-time event from your site or app (form, payment, signup): Webhook or the app's instant trigger.
- "When X appears in this SaaS tool": the app's trigger node.
- Reusable helper other workflows call: Execute Sub-workflow trigger.
- Handling failures: Error Trigger (we will get there).

Pick the trigger that matches how the real world produces the event. Get this right and the rest of the workflow almost designs itself.

lessons.title: Nodes and How Data Flows
lessons.bodyMd:
## Items: the currency of n8n

Data moves between nodes as items. An item is a JSON object. A node that receives five items runs its operation five times, once per item, automatically. This is the single most important thing to internalize: you do not need a loop to process a list. If your HTTP node returns 50 rows, the next node handles all 50 on its own.

## Reading the inspector

After a test run, click any node. The INPUT panel shows the items that arrived; the OUTPUT panel shows what left. Each item looks like:

```json
{
  "name": "Maya Chen",
  "email": "maya@example.com",
  "plan": "pro"
}
```

n8n wraps each in a small envelope internally, but in expressions and Code nodes you work with the clean JSON above via `$json`.

## The Set node: shaping data by hand

The Set node builds or reshapes items without code. Give it assignments like:

- `fullName` = `={{ $json.firstName }} {{ $json.lastName }}`
- `email` = `={{ $json.email.toLowerCase().trim() }}`
- `isPro` = `={{ $json.plan === "pro" }}`

Use Set when the transformation is simple field mapping. It is visual, readable, and easy for teammates to understand.

## The Code node: full power when you need it

When logic gets complex (grouping, filtering, math, reformatting), the Code node runs JavaScript. The default mode is "Run Once for All Items": your code receives every item at once and returns the new list.

```js
// Keep only pro-plan customers, add a greeting
const pros = $input.all().filter(item => item.json.plan === "pro");

return pros.map(item => ({
  json: {
    email: item.json.email,
    greeting: `Hi ${item.json.name}, thanks for being a pro member.`
  }
}));
```

Key helpers: `$input.all()` returns all items, `$input.first()` returns the first. Always return an array of `{ json: {...} }` objects. That return shape is the contract: whatever you return becomes the items flowing downstream.

## The mode gotcha

The Code node has two modes, and mixing them up causes the most common beginner bug:

- **Run Once for All Items** (default): your code runs a single time and sees everything. Use for filtering, grouping, aggregating.
- **Run Once for Each Item**: your code runs once per item, and `$json` refers to the current item. Use for per-item transforms.

If your output has the wrong number of items (one when you expected fifty, or fifty when you expected one), check the mode first. This single check resolves a huge fraction of "weird behavior" reports.

## HTTP Request: the universal adapter

With 400+ built-in integrations, n8n still cannot cover every API. The HTTP Request node covers the rest. Set the method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), the URL, headers, and body, and you can talk to anything with a REST API.

```text
Method: POST
URL: https://api.example.com/contacts
Headers: Authorization: Bearer YOUR_KEY (use a credential, never paste keys here)
Body (JSON): { "email": "={{ $json.email }}", "name": "={{ $json.name }}" }
```

Notice the `={{ ... }}` expressions inside the body: static structure, dynamic values. That combination is the heart of practical n8n work.

## Putting it together: a lead router

A realistic small workflow: Webhook trigger (form submission) → Code node (normalize: lowercase email, trim whitespace, derive company domain) → HTTP Request (look the domain up in your CRM or enrichment API) → IF node (route hot leads one way, others another way) → Slack message to the team. Four node types, one useful automation. You now know every piece of it except the IF node, which is next lesson's... actually, two lessons from now. First, expressions.

lessons.title: Expressions: Making Data Dynamic
lessons.bodyMd:
## What expressions are

Expressions are the `{{ }}` placeholders you put inside node fields. They let a field's value be computed from the workflow's data instead of typed in by hand. Static text says the same thing every run; expressions say something different for every item.

```text
To:      {{ $json.email }}
Subject: Welcome, {{ $json.firstName }}!
Body:    Your plan ({{ $json.plan }}) renews on {{ $json.renewalDate }}.
```

One email node, personalized for every customer, automatically.

## The variables you will use constantly

- `$json`  -  the current item's data. `{{ $json.email }}`, `{{ $json.address.city }}`.
- `$input`  -  all incoming items and helpers: `$input.first().json`, `$input.all()`.
- `$node["Node Name"]`  -  reach back to a specific earlier node's output: `{{ $node["Webhook"].json["email"] }}`. Useful when the data you need is several steps upstream.
- `$now` and `$today`  -  the current date/time, for timestamps and scheduling math.
- `$env`  -  environment variables on self-hosted instances: `{{ $env.API_KEY }}`. Never hardcode secrets when `$env` exists.
- `$workflow`  -  metadata like the workflow name and id.

## JavaScript inside the braces

Between `{{ }}` you can run real JavaScript: method calls, ternaries, math.

```text
{{ $json.email.toLowerCase().trim() }}
{{ $json.quantity * $json.unitPrice }}
{{ $json.plan === "pro" ? "Priority support" : "Community support" }}
{{ $json.tags.includes("vip") ? "VIP" : "Standard" }}
{{ new Date($json.createdAt).toLocaleDateString() }}
```

## The drag-and-drop shortcut

You rarely need to memorize paths. In any field, the input panel shows the incoming data with a draggable schema. Drag a field into your text and n8n writes the expression for you. Learn by dragging first, then start typing them by hand as the patterns become familiar.

## Common expression mistakes

**Forgetting which item you are on.** `$json` is the current item. If a node received 10 items, the expression evaluates 10 times, once per item. That is usually what you want.

**Reaching across branches incorrectly.** After an IF node splits the flow, `$json` on each branch refers to that branch's items. To grab data from before the split, use `$node["Earlier Node"].json`.

**Null values crashing a chain.** `{{ $json.address.city }}` throws if `address` is missing. Defensive version: `{{ $json.address?.city ?? "Unknown" }}`. The `?.` and `??` operators are your friends with messy real-world data.

**Date confusion.** APIs return dates as strings like `"2026-09-16T14:30:00Z"`. Wrap in `new Date(...)` before formatting or comparing.

## When to use expressions vs. a Code node

Rule of thumb: if the logic fits in one line per field, use expressions. If you need loops, multiple steps, or intermediate variables, use a Code node. Expressions are for wiring data; Code nodes are for thinking with data. Both are first-class, and mixing them freely is normal.

Practice: open your morning briefing workflow, and rewrite the Code node's message using a Set node with expressions instead. Feel both tools. You will reach for each one dozens of times a day once you are building seriously.

lessons.title: Branching and Looping: IF, Switch, Merge
lessons.bodyMd:
## Routing with IF

The IF node splits your flow into two paths: true and false. It asks one question about each item and routes accordingly.

Example: after your webhook receives a lead, add an IF node with the condition `plan` equals `pro`. Pro leads flow down the true branch (Slack alert to sales, priority task in CRM). Everyone else flows down the false branch (welcome email sequence).

Conditions can combine: AND/OR groups, comparisons (equals, contains, greater than), and expression-powered checks like `{{ $json.score >= 80 }}`. Keep conditions deterministic and readable. If you cannot explain the rule in one sentence, it probably belongs in a Code node instead.

## Routing with Switch

When two branches are not enough, the Switch node routes to one of many outputs based on a value. Example: route support tickets by `priority` (low, medium, high, urgent) to four different handling paths, or route by `region` to the right team. Switch keeps multi-way routing in one tidy node instead of a chain of IFs.

## Combining streams with Merge

Sooner or later you need to bring branches back together or combine data from two sources. The Merge node has several modes; the three you will use:

- **Append:** stack items from both inputs into one list. Two lists of contacts become one list.
- **Combine:** join items by matching fields, like a database join. Enrichment data meets the original record on `email`.
- **Choose Branch:** pass through one input or the other based on a condition.

Pick the mode deliberately. The most common Merge confusion is item counts: if input 1 has 10 items and input 2 has 3, know which side wins in your chosen mode, and check the output inspector to confirm.

One historical gotcha worth knowing: in very old workflows using the legacy execution order, a Merge placed after an IF could cause both branches to execute. Modern workflows use the current execution order and do not have this problem, but if you ever inherit an ancient workflow that behaves strangely around merges, check its execution order setting.

## Looping with Loop Over Items

Remember: n8n processes items automatically, so you do not need a loop to handle a list. Use the Loop Over Items node only when you need explicit batch control:

- **Rate limits:** an API allows 10 requests per second, so process items in batches of 10 with a Wait node between batches.
- **Batch APIs:** the destination wants records in groups of 100.
- **Process-all-then-continue:** do something for every item, then continue the workflow only after all batches finish.

The loop has two outputs: "done" (each batch, loop back into your processing nodes) and "finished" (fires once when all items are processed; continue the rest of the workflow from here).

## A realistic pattern: batched enrichment

Webhook receives 500 new contacts → Loop Over Items (batch size 50) → HTTP Request to enrichment API (50 per call) → Wait 1 second (respect rate limits) → loop back → when finished, Merge results → write to CRM. This pattern handles volume gracefully instead of hammering the API with 500 simultaneous requests.

## Debugging checklist for weird flow behavior

When a workflow with branches and loops misbehaves, check in this order:

1. Item counts between nodes (does each node receive what you expect?).
2. Code node mode (Run Once for All Items vs. Each Item).
3. Merge mode and which input wins.
4. Whether pagination or batching is dropping data.
5. Reproduce with pinned data before changing anything.

This checklist resolves the vast majority of logic bugs. You now own the core building blocks. Next chapter: we add brains.

lessons.title: Adding an LLM to Your Workflow
lessons.bodyMd:
## From fixed logic to flexible thinking

Everything so far has been deterministic: if X, do Y. That handles most automation beautifully. But some tasks need judgment: summarizing a messy email thread, categorizing free-text feedback, drafting a personalized reply. That is where LLM nodes come in. You keep your reliable pipeline; you just add a thinking step where thinking is actually needed.

## Connecting a model

AI nodes need a model credential. In the Credentials panel, add your provider: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or a local model via Ollama (self-hosted only, great for privacy). One credential can serve every AI node in every workflow.

Cost note for beginners: start with a cheap, fast model (like GPT-4o-mini or Claude Haiku) for high-volume tasks. Reserve the big models for work where quality visibly matters. You can swap models later without rebuilding the workflow.

## Your first LLM step: the information extractor

The simplest useful AI pattern is extraction: turn unstructured text into structured data. Add an "Information Extractor" node (under AI nodes), connect your model, and define the fields you want:

```json
{
  "name": "string",
  "email": "string",
  "urgency": "low | medium | high",
  "summary": "string"
}
```

Feed it a support email. Out comes clean JSON your downstream nodes can route on. The email said "this is kind of urgent, my checkout is broken" in three rambling paragraphs; your workflow now has `urgency: "high"` as a reliable field. Deterministic routing on AI-extracted structure is one of the highest-value patterns in automation.

## Summarization: the digest workflow

A classic beginner AI workflow: RSS Read node pulls the latest posts from a few feeds → an LLM summarization node condenses each item to two sentences → Code node assembles a digest → email or Slack delivers it every morning.

The summarizer prompt matters more than the model. Be specific:

```text
Summarize the following article in exactly two sentences.
Focus on what changed and why it matters.
Do not add opinions. Article: {{ $json.content }}
```

Constraints ("exactly two sentences", "do not add opinions") dramatically improve consistency. Vague prompts produce vague outputs.

## Sentiment and classification

Another bread-and-butter pattern: classify incoming items so your deterministic logic can act. A Code node cannot reliably tell whether a review is angry; an LLM can. Chain it: LLM classifies `sentiment: positive | neutral | negative` → IF node routes negatives to a human immediately, positives to a testimonial candidate list. The AI does the judgment; the workflow does the reliable routing. This division of labor is the theme of the whole chapter.

## Prompt hygiene basics

- **Be explicit about format.** Ask for JSON when downstream nodes need fields. Show the schema.
- **Give examples.** One input/output example beats three paragraphs of description.
- **Constrain length.** "In under 50 words" prevents runaway outputs that break your layouts.
- **Separate instructions from data.** Label clearly: `Instructions: ... Article: {{ $json.content }}`. This reduces prompt-injection weirdness from untrusted input.
- **Test with real data.** Your five prettiest test cases are not your real data. Run the ugliest real examples through before activating.

## What not to do yet

Do not let an LLM make irreversible decisions unsupervised: sending emails, deleting records, charging cards. In this lesson the LLM only produces text and structured data; humans or deterministic gates still decide what happens next. Chapter 4's later lessons add agents with tools, and Lesson 4 adds the guardrails that keep them safe. For now, enjoy the superpower: judgment as a workflow step.

lessons.title: Building Your First AI Agent
lessons.bodyMd:
## What an AI agent actually is

An agent is an LLM that can use tools. Instead of just generating text, it decides which tools to call, in what order, to accomplish a goal. In n8n, the AI Agent node is the brain; you plug in a chat model, a memory, and one or more tools. The agent reasons: "The user asked about their order. I should look it up with the order-lookup tool, then answer."

The current n8n agent operates as a Tools Agent: it must have at least one tool connected, or it has nothing to act with.

## The anatomy of an agent node

- **Chat model (sub-node):** the LLM doing the reasoning. Start with a capable mid-tier model.
- **Memory (sub-node):** lets the agent remember conversation context across messages. For chat workflows, window memory (last N messages) is the simple default.
- **Tools (sub-nodes):** the capabilities. Calculator, HTTP requests, Code execution, Wikipedia, and most powerfully, your own workflows exposed as tools.
- **System message:** the agent's job description and rules. This is the most important field you will write.

## Tools you can give it

n8n ships tool versions of many nodes. The standouts for beginners:

- **Calculator:** safe arithmetic the LLM should not do in its head.
- **HTTP Request Tool:** call any API.
- **Code Tool:** run JavaScript for data shaping.
- **Call n8n Workflow Tool:** run another workflow and get its result. This is the big one: any reliable workflow you have built (order lookup, CRM search, FAQ search) becomes a tool the agent can invoke by name.

## Build: a support triage agent

Goal: a chat agent that answers common questions from your docs and escalates the rest to a human.

1. Add a Chat Trigger (so you can talk to it in the n8n chat window).
2. Add an AI Agent node. Connect a chat model and window memory.
3. Add a "Call n8n Workflow Tool" pointing at a small sub-workflow: it takes a `question`, searches your FAQ data, and returns the best match. Name the tool clearly: `search_faq`.
4. Write the system message:

```text
You are a support assistant for Acme Inc.
Use the search_faq tool to answer questions about our product.
If the tool returns no good match, say: "I don't have a confident
answer for that, so I'm escalating you to our team." Then call the
escalate_to_human tool with the user's question.
Never invent product details. Never promise refunds or discounts.
```

5. Add a second workflow tool, `escalate_to_human`, that posts the question to Slack.

Test in the chat window. Ask something in the FAQ, then something obscure. Watch the agent call tools and explain itself.

## Writing good tool descriptions

The agent decides when to use a tool based on its description. Write descriptions like contracts, not slogans.

Bad: "Use this for CRM."
Good: "Use this tool to create or update a HubSpot note after a meeting summary is approved. Input must include contact ID, company ID if known, note body, and meeting date."

Tell the model exactly when to use the tool, what inputs it needs, and what it returns.

## The first-item gotcha

One official quirk to know: inside AI sub-nodes (like workflow tools), expressions resolve against the first input item, not each item. If your tool behaves as if it only sees one record when many arrive, reshape the data upstream so the tool receives exactly what it needs. Do not assume multi-item expressions work the same inside sub-nodes as they do at the top level.

## Start narrow

Your first agent should have two or three tools and one clear job. Agents with fifteen tools and vague goals wander, burn tokens, and make mistakes. Nail the narrow version, then expand. In the next lesson, we give the agent real knowledge with RAG.

lessons.title: RAG Basics: Giving AI Your Data
lessons.bodyMd:
## The problem RAG solves

LLMs know the public internet up to their training cutoff. They do not know your product docs, your pricing, your policies, or your meeting notes. You could paste documents into every prompt, but that gets expensive and hits context limits fast.

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) fixes this: store your documents as searchable vectors, retrieve only the relevant chunks for each question, and hand those chunks to the LLM. The agent answers from your data, not its imagination.

## The pipeline in plain English

1. **Load** your documents (Google Docs, PDFs, Notion pages, website URLs).
2. **Split** them into chunks (a few hundred words each; chunks are the unit of retrieval).
3. **Embed** each chunk (turn text into a vector, a list of numbers capturing meaning).
4. **Store** the vectors in a vector database (Supabase, Pinecone, Qdrant, or n8n's in-memory store for experiments).
5. At question time, **retrieve** the most similar chunks and stuff them into the prompt.

In n8n, steps 1-4 are a one-time (or scheduled) indexing workflow. Step 5 happens live inside your agent via a retriever tool.

## Building the indexer workflow

A simple version: Manual trigger → Default Data Loader (point it at your docs or URLs) → Recursive Character Text Splitter (chunk size ~1000 characters, overlap ~200) → Embeddings (OpenAI or another provider) → Supabase Vector Store (insert mode). Run it once. Your documents are now searchable.

Re-run the indexer on a schedule (weekly, or when docs change) with the vector store in upsert mode so updated documents replace old chunks instead of duplicating them.

## Wiring retrieval into your agent

In your agent workflow, add a "Vector Store Retriever" tool connected to the same Supabase collection. Give it a crisp description:

```text
Use this tool to search Acme's product documentation.
Input: the user's question as a search query.
Returns: the most relevant documentation chunks.
Always check here before answering product questions.
```

Now the agent's loop is: user asks → agent searches your docs → agent answers grounded in retrieved text. Ask it something only your docs know. Then ask something your docs do not cover, and confirm it says it does not know rather than inventing an answer.

## Chunking and retrieval tips

- **Chunks too big** dilute relevance; **too small** lose context. Start around 500-1000 characters with overlap.
- **Metadata matters.** Store source titles and URLs with each chunk so the agent can cite where answers came from.
- **Test retrieval separately.** Before blaming the agent for a bad answer, check what the retriever returned. Most RAG failures are retrieval failures, not model failures.
- **Keep the index fresh.** Stale docs produce confidently wrong answers. Schedule re-indexing.

## The honest limits

RAG reduces hallucination; it does not eliminate it. Retrieved chunks can be misread, and the model can still fill gaps with plausible fiction. For high-stakes answers (pricing, legal, medical), keep a human in the loop or restrict the agent to quoting retrieved text verbatim. RAG is a massive upgrade over "the model guesses," but it is not a truth machine. Next lesson: the guardrails that keep all of this safe.

lessons.title: AI Guardrails: When Not to Use an Agent
lessons.bodyMd:
## The core principle

Use AI where judgment is needed; use deterministic logic everywhere else. An agent should never be doing a job that a simple IF node or API call could do. Every agentic step you add costs latency, money, and auditability. Spend that budget only where reasoning earns its keep.

**Prefer deterministic when:** the route is obvious, the rules are fixed, the operation is a straightforward API call, or auditability matters more than adaptability. Routing, CRUD, validation, and scoring with clear thresholds are code jobs.

**Use an agent when:** tool choice depends on context, the input is messy natural language, research or synthesis is required, or the workflow must reason over incomplete information. Triage, summarization, drafting, and conversational help are agent jobs.

## The approval pattern

The single most important safety pattern: let the agent prepare, but make a human approve before anything irreversible happens. n8n supports tool-level human approval. The pattern:

1. Agent drafts the action (an email, a CRM update, a refund).
2. Workflow sends the exact tool name and parameters to a reviewer via Slack, email, or chat.
3. Reviewer approves or denies.
4. On approve, the workflow executes. On deny, control returns to the agent with a graceful fallback ("The reviewer declined; suggest an alternative.").

Use human review whenever tools send external communications, modify production records, or take actions you cannot undo. Drafting is AI-speed; sending is human-gated.

## Narrow the blast radius

- **Smallest useful tool set.** Give the agent only the tools it needs. An agent that can read tickets does not need the tool that deletes customers.
- **Read before write.** Separate research workflows (read-only, safe to run freely) from execution workflows (writes, gated). Let the agent research broadly and act narrowly.
- **Narrow tool descriptions.** As Lesson 2 showed, precise contracts beat vague ones. Also tell the agent what NOT to do in the system message: "Never promise refunds. Never invent product details."
- **Fail closed.** If the agent is unsure, the default path should be escalation to a human, not a guess. Write that default into the system prompt explicitly.

## Evaluate before you change

AI behavior drifts when you change prompts, models, or tool descriptions. n8n's official guidance recommends two stages: light evaluation on a small dataset while iterating, and metric-based evaluation after deployment.

Practical version for beginners:

1. Collect 5-20 representative examples (real questions, real inputs).
2. Record what good output looks like for each.
3. Re-run the set every time you change the prompt or model.
4. Add every real-world failure to the set as a new edge case.

This takes an hour to set up and saves you from the classic disaster: "we tweaked the prompt and support quality quietly got worse for three weeks."

## Watch the failure modes

- **Tool confusion:** the agent picks the wrong tool. Fix with better descriptions and fewer tools.
- **Context bloat:** long conversations eat the context window and the agent forgets instructions. Fix with tighter memory windows and summarization.
- **Silent degradation:** outputs get slightly worse over time. Fix with the evaluation set above.
- **Cost surprise:** an agent looping on tools can burn serious tokens. Set max iterations on the agent node and monitor execution costs.

## The checklist before activating any AI workflow

- Deterministic parts are deterministic; the agent does only the judgment parts.
- Human approval gates every irreversible action.
- The system prompt states what the agent must never do.
- An evaluation set exists and passes.
- Max iterations and timeouts are set.
- You have watched it handle your ugliest real inputs, not just the pretty ones.

AI makes n8n dramatically more capable. Guardrails make it safe to leave running. Final chapter: keeping everything healthy in production.

lessons.title: Reading Executions Like a Detective
lessons.bodyMd:
## Executions are the flight recorder

Every run of every workflow is recorded on the Executions tab: when it ran, whether it succeeded, how long it took, and exactly what each node did. When something goes wrong at 2 AM, executions tell you precisely what happened. Learn to read them and you can debug anything.

## Reading an execution

Open Executions, click a run. You see the workflow canvas with each node marked: green for success, red for failure. Click any node to see its input and output for that run, exactly as it was. The run stops at the failing node, so the red node is where your investigation starts, and its error message is the first clue.

Execution statuses you will see:

- **Success:** everything completed.
- **Error:** a node failed. The error message names the node and the reason.
- **Waiting:** the workflow paused at a Wait node or is awaiting human approval. This is normal, not broken.
- **Canceled:** someone stopped it manually.

## The five-minute debug routine

1. **Read the error message literally.** "404 Not Found" means the URL is wrong. "Authentication failed" means the credential is wrong or expired. Beginners skim errors; experts read them word by word.
2. **Check the node's input.** Click the red node, open INPUT. Was the data what you expected? Half of all bugs are upstream: the failing node is innocent, it just received garbage.
3. **Check item counts.** Did the node receive 0 items? Then it never really ran; the problem is earlier. Did it receive 1,000 when you expected 10? Then a branch or merge multiplied your data.
4. **Isolate with a manual run.** Copy the failing section into a test, pin the input data (right-click the node output, "Pin data"), and execute just that node repeatedly while you fix it. Pinned data means you are not re-firing webhooks or re-calling APIs on every test.
5. **Check the usual suspects:** Code node mode (All Items vs. Each Item), expression typos (`$json.emial` fails silently into undefined), expired credentials, and API rate limits.

## Debugging data issues vs. logic issues

Data issues: the workflow is correct but the data is surprising (null fields, unexpected formats, empty responses). Fix by making nodes defensive: `?.` optional chaining in expressions, IF nodes that check for required fields, Code nodes that validate before transforming.

Logic issues: the data is fine but the routing is wrong (items going down the wrong branch, loops not terminating). Fix by tracing item counts node by node and re-reading your conditions. Add a temporary Set node that labels items ("I came from branch A") to make flow visible.

## The executions list as a health dashboard

Beyond individual bugs, scan the executions list regularly: rising error rates, executions taking longer than usual, workflows that stopped running entirely (a schedule trigger with no recent executions means something changed). n8n's built-in Insights dashboard shows production executions, failure rate, and average run time at a glance. Make checking it a weekly habit, like checking your bank balance.

## When to ask for help

If you have pinned data reproducing the bug, the exact error message, and the item counts at each step, you can get help fast: n8n's community forum is excellent, and a well-described problem ("node X receives these 3 items, produces this error") gets answered quickly. "My workflow is broken" does not. The debug routine above is really just the discipline of gathering the facts that make help possible.

Next: making failures handle themselves, so 2 AM pages become rare.

lessons.title: Error Handling That Actually Works
lessons.bodyMd:
## Two layers of defense

Reliable workflows need two things: per-node resilience (handle the hiccup and keep going) and workflow-level safety nets (when something truly fails, fail loudly and cleanly). n8n gives you both.

## Layer 1: retries and error outputs

Every node has Settings with retry options. For nodes calling external APIs, turn on retry: 3 attempts with exponential backoff handles the vast majority of transient failures (rate limits, brief outages, network blips). This one setting eliminates most "it failed at 2 AM for no reason" incidents.

Each node also has an "On Error" behavior:

- **Stop Workflow (default):** fail the execution. Right for most cases; you want to know.
- **Continue (regular output):** pretend it succeeded and keep going. Dangerous unless you genuinely do not care about the result.
- **Continue (error output):** route to a separate error output you wire to fallback logic. Powerful: "if enrichment fails, continue with unenriched data and flag it."

Example: your lead workflow enriches via an API. Set retry to 3 with backoff, and On Error to continue with error output wired to a path that marks the lead `enrichment_failed: true` and still notifies sales. The lead never gets lost because one API hiccuped.

## Layer 2: the error workflow

In Workflow Settings, you can assign an error workflow: a separate workflow that runs automatically whenever this one fails. It must start with an Error Trigger node, which receives the failure details: which workflow, which node, the error message, the execution id.

One error workflow can serve many workflows. A solid default error workflow:

1. Error Trigger receives the failure.
2. Code node formats an alert: workflow name, failed node, error message, execution link.
3. IF node: is this the third failure in an hour? (Track counts in a simple store or just alert every time while you are small.)
4. Slack/Email node posts the alert to your team channel with a link to the execution.

Now failures wake you up with context instead of silence.

## Failing deliberately with Stop and Error

Sometimes the right move is to fail on purpose. The Stop and Error node lets you halt with your own message when business rules are violated: "Lead rejected: email failed deliverability check," or "Halted: duplicate customer detected, not creating a second record."

Why fail instead of silently skipping? Because deliberate failures route into your error workflow, creating a visible record. Silent skips hide problems. Detect invalid state early, fail with a clear custom message, and let your alerting do its job.

## Timeouts and stuck workflows

In Workflow Settings, set a timeout (e.g., 5 minutes for most workflows). A workflow that hangs forever on an unresponsive API holds resources and confuses monitoring. Timeouts turn hangs into clean failures, which your error workflow then reports.

For human-approval steps that might wait hours, that is what the Wait node and approval patterns are for: waiting is a designed state, not a stuck one.

## A reliability checklist per workflow

Before activating anything that matters:

- Retries enabled on every external API call (3 attempts, exponential backoff).
- On Error behavior chosen deliberately per node, not left on default blindly.
- An error workflow assigned in Workflow Settings.
- Timeout set.
- Deliberate Stop and Error nodes at your business-rule gates (bad data in, no silent processing).
- You have triggered a failure on purpose and watched the alert arrive.

Do a fire drill: break something intentionally (bad credential, invalid URL), run it, and confirm the alert lands in Slack with the right details. The best time to discover your alerting is broken is during a drill, not during a real outage.

lessons.title: Credentials, Secrets, and Staying Secure
lessons.bodyMd:
## Credentials: the vault

The Credentials section in the sidebar is n8n's vault. Each credential stores one login: an API key, OAuth connection, database password, or SMTP account. Workflows reference credentials by name and never see the raw secret. This separation is the foundation of everything below.

Rules that are not optional:

1. **Never paste secrets into node fields.** If a field wants an API key, it wants a credential. Pasting a raw key into a workflow means it gets exported with the workflow JSON, visible to anyone who can view the workflow.
2. **One credential per purpose.** A shared "OpenAI" credential for all workflows is fine; a single API key pasted into twelve workflows is a rotation nightmare.
3. **Name credentials clearly.** "OpenAI - Production" beats "My Key 3". Future you rotates keys at midnight; clear names save you.
4. **Rotate on suspicion.** If a key might have leaked (pasted in chat, committed to git, shown on a screenshare), rotate it immediately at the provider, then update the one credential in n8n. Because workflows reference the credential, not the key, rotation is a one-place fix.

## Environment variables on self-hosted

For values that vary between environments or should never appear in the UI, use environment variables and reference them as `{{ $env.MY_SECRET }}` in expressions. Webhook secrets, internal tokens, and feature flags live here. Keep a documented list of required variables alongside your compose file so a fresh install is reproducible.

## Webhook security, revisited

From Chapter 3, the short version for production: every inbound webhook that triggers real actions gets authentication (header or basic auth in the Webhook node settings), or signature verification in the first Code node. Test URLs are for building; production URLs are for live traffic; never mix them up in your external systems.

## Who can see what

On n8n Cloud and multi-user self-hosted setups, workflows and credentials have sharing settings. Principle of least privilege: people see the workflows they operate, credentials are shared only where needed. If you are a solo builder today, still name and organize things as if a teammate joins tomorrow.

## Backups are security too

Ransomware, accidental deletion, a bad import overwriting a working workflow: exports are your time machine. Monthly (or after every significant change): export critical workflows as JSON and commit them to a private git repo. On self-hosted, back up the data volume as shown in Chapter 2. Test a restore once. An untested backup is a rumor.

## The five-minute security audit

Run through this quarterly:

- No raw secrets in any workflow JSON (export one and search for key-like strings).
- All production webhooks authenticated.
- Credentials named clearly; no mystery entries.
- n8n updated to a recent version (security fixes ship regularly).
- Backups exist and a restore was tested at least once.
- Former teammates' access revoked.

Security in n8n is mostly discipline, not cleverness. The vault exists; use it, name things well, and rotate without drama. Final lesson: the habits that separate tinkering from production.

lessons.title: Going Further: Best Practices and Next Steps
lessons.bodyMd:
## Build like you will maintain it

The difference between a workflow that survives and one that rots is not cleverness. It is boring habits, applied consistently.

**Name everything.** Nodes default to names like "HTTP Request1". Rename to "Enrich via Apollo" and "Slack alert to #sales". Six months from now, the canvas should read like a story.

**Document with sticky notes.** Right-click the canvas, add a note, and explain the why: "We check HubSpot first to avoid emailing existing customers. Do not remove." The what is visible; the why evaporates.

**One workflow, one job.** A 60-node monster that does lead routing, reporting, and birthday emails is unmaintainable. Split by responsibility and connect pieces with the Execute Sub-workflow node. Small workflows are testable, reusable, and debuggable.

**Sub-workflows for repeated capabilities.** Enrichment, CRM lookups, notification formatting, approval routing: if you build it twice, extract it into a sub-workflow with a clear input contract. Define the expected input fields in the sub-workflow's trigger so callers know the deal.

## Change safely

**Version in git.** Export workflow JSON into a repo before significant changes. n8n does not have built-in version history worth relying on; git does.

**Test with pinned data.** Before changing a live workflow, pin real input data at the top, duplicate the workflow, and experiment on the copy. Promote the copy when it behaves.

**Evaluate AI changes.** From Chapter 4: every prompt, model, or tool change gets run against your evaluation set before release. No exceptions for "small" tweaks.

**Roll out gradually for high-impact workflows.** Run the new version alongside the old on a subset of traffic (a canary), watch failure rates, then cut over. For workflows that send money or emails, this is not paranoia; it is professionalism.

## Know your numbers

n8n's Insights dashboard gives you production executions, failure rate, time saved, and average run time. Add workflow-specific metrics where it matters: for a lead workflow, track lead-to-owner latency and CRM writeback success. Numbers turn "I think it is working" into "I know."
